title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
hook: sick and ready to give all his wealth away, he was told: a third is plenty (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Awf, who turned down half a fortune and asked for the market. Your line was rich and giving.

A man lies sick in Mecca, so sick he fears he will die there. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes to visit. And the sick man, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, has a plan ready. I have a lot of wealth, he says, and only one daughter to inherit from me. Shall I give two thirds of it away in charity? No. Half, then? No. A third? A third, the Prophet says, and a third is a lot. Today: a generous man stopped, kindly, from being too generous.
screen: `SICK IN MECCA.` → `TWO THIRDS? HALF?` → `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Sa'd tells this himself, in Sahih al-Bukhari. He is ill and wants to do the most good he can with what he has left. The Prophet doesn't say: wonderful, give it all. He bargains him down, and then gives the reason, the heart of the day. It is better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them poor, holding out their hands to people. The daughter matters. Charity that leaves your own people begging has missed something. Then a second line, just as surprising: whatever you spend seeking God's pleasure, you are rewarded for it, even the bite of food you lift to your wife's mouth. So feeding your family is not the opposite of charity. It counts. Sa'd also feared dying in Mecca, the city he had left when he emigrated. The Prophet told him he might live on, so that some people would benefit through him and others be harmed. Tradition says he did live on. Muslim jurists use this visit as a foundation for the rule that a person may leave no more than a third of their estate as a bequest, with the rest passing to heirs by the shares the Qur'an sets. Different schools work out the details differently, but the third is traced back to this room. Generous enough to matter. Careful enough to leave no one behind.
screen: `A GENEROUS MAN, BARGAINED DOWN.` · `BETTER TO LEAVE YOUR HEIRS WELL OFF.` · `EVEN THE BITE TO YOUR WIFE'S MOUTH.` · `WHY A BEQUEST STOPS AT A THIRD.` · then, large: `A THIRD IS PLENTY.`

segments.voice: Think of the places where you give: money, time, energy, attention. Look honestly for one where you give so much that the people closest to you go without, or one where you give nothing at all, and picture one small adjustment. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom in giving.
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. The companion who, sick in Mecca, wanted to give away most of his wealth, and was told a third is a lot, and that feeding his family counts too. Today's word.
Your line: a third is plenty. Feeding your own family counts too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Islamic law a person may leave up to a third of their estate as a bequest, for charity or for people outside the fixed shares; the rest passes to heirs by the shares set in the Qur'an. Schools differ on the details.

chat.says: Is it more religious to give away almost everything you own?
options: Not always: the Prophet stopped Sa'd at a third, for his heirs' sake.
Yes; the Prophet praised Sa'd for wanting to give two thirds away.
Yes; leaving heirs well off matters less than any act of charity.
chat.meaning: A third, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than poor; even feeding your family is rewarded.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.meaning: an emigrant companion who asked how much to give away

Mecca.meaning: the city Sa'd had left when he emigrated

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2742 / 1295 / 5354 (Sa'd's illness; two thirds, half, a third; 'a third is a lot'; heirs well off; the bite to your wife's mouth)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm. Some versions place the visit during the Farewell Pilgrimage, others at the conquest of Mecca; the script says only 'in Mecca'.
'A third is a lot' renders al-thuluth kathir; the index carry says 'a third is plenty'. Confirm the gloss.

The one-third bequest limit (wasiyyah) as a legal principle drawn from this hadith is stated generally; not in the hadith text itself. Keeper to confirm the framing 'Muslim jurists use it as a foundation' and 'different schools work out the details differently'.
'The report shows he did live on' relies on the narration being told later by Sa'd himself; confirm or soften.
